about: Real people who lived or worked in Kowloon Walled City (九龍城寨), each from a published source in the repo. This file is separate from the rooms (data/room_uses.json): linked_facts gives the ids of data/room_research.json for the places where each person lived or worked. nameZh is given only where a source prints the Chinese name. in_dec_1986 is true if the source shows the person in the City in December 1986, false if it shows that they were not, and null if the source gives no date. The people of the GRS clearance files (政府檔案處, HKRS1255-3) come from the catalogue entries of the files: their stories give only what the catalogue gives. A check on 2026-11-05 compared each of the 230 quotes with its source: each press quote with the saved text of its article, each book quote with an OCR of the cited page scan, and each GRS quote with the research facts. All match. People sweep 2 (2026-11-06) added people from the press, books, archives and the Chinese media: each quote was checked by machine against its web page or a saved copy, and each quote of the 2014 book against the OCR of the cited page. A source that failed the check was dropped. details gives one fact per item, with the index of its source in sources; inferred marks the researcher's inference. related links the people of one family or workplace. lived_or_worked tells if the person lived in the City, worked there, or both. leads lists the people that the sources name but do not yet prove.

people.name: Lam Mei Kwong
people.story: Lam Mei Kwong was a dentist in the Walled City. He arrived in the City in 1949. A photo shows him in his dental clinic at 4A Lung Shing Road (龍城路). The caption calls the clinic spacious by Walled City standards. He occupied that address almost continuously from 1949. His dental equipment appeared to date from the same period. The caption says that it was possibly imported second-hand from Japan. The book's map of the late 1980s lists him as a retired dentist, at number 19. The book has no interview with him. Only the photo caption on page 11 and the map index tell his story.

people.name: Yau Lap Cheong
people.story: Yau Lap Cheong came from Chiu Yeung, in China, in 1928, at the age of 20. He lived near and in the Walled City from then until 1990. He first worked as a foreman in a clothing factory. Then a friend handed him a business that sold cigarettes to gamblers. He took over a store and rented its space of about 70 square feet for $6 a month. His brothers joined him. The street had a dance hall, gambling dens and opium dens. The store was open 24 hours a day and used gaslights. His younger brother gambled and sold heroin for a time. Yau quit the store five or six years before the interview of about 1990. He then lived alone in a one-room flat with no windows. He rarely went out and listened to Cantonese opera on the radio. He also owned a fifth-floor flat that paid him $1000 a month in rent. He moved out in 1990, in the first phase of the clearance.

people.name: Ho Chi Kam
people.story: Ho Chi Kam was a barber. He read about a flat in the Sing Pao Daily News (成報) and bought it. He moved in at the start of 1974. The flat was on Tung Tau Tsuen Road (東頭村道), thus he had no reason to go inside the City. The book says that he lived in the City long before 1985. Before 1985 he worked as a barber for other people. Then a friend offered him the barber's shop at 10 Tai Chang Street (大井街). He borrowed money and took it over in 1985. After that he came into the City every day. The shop stood near the only Government standpipe inside the City. He and his wife both worked there. Most customers were local residents, and the shop was cheaper than barbers outside. When the City was to be demolished, he went back to work for others. He came to the shop only on Wednesdays, his day off. The shop closed in 1991.

people.name: Wong Yu Ming
people.story: Wong Yu Ming was born in 1930. He studied medicine in China. He learnt dentistry and herbal medicine from his father, a dentist, and by his own study. The Communist Party said that he had bad thoughts. Thus he left Chiu Chow (潮州) for Hong Kong in the late 1950s. He came alone, and his wife and children followed. After a few months he rented premises on Lung Shing Road (龍城路) and opened a dental clinic. He bought the premises a year later. He extracted teeth, did fillings and made false teeth. He often made dentures under contract for registered dentists outside the City. Once he had three employees, but by the interview they had left. His wife, Cheung Mei, learnt the trade from him and was his dental assistant. He worked and lived in the clinic 24 hours a day. His seven children lived with their mother in her flat elsewhere. He felt lonely.

people.name: Hui Kwong
people.story: Hui Kwong came from Malaya. As a young man he went to China to support the war against Japan. A few years after 1945 he came to Hong Kong, but he had no valid passport. He then ran a travel agency in China and married at 30. When private businesses closed, he got out to Macau. In 1965 he brought his wife and daughter to Hong Kong. Life was hard, and the family found a cheaper place in the Walled City. The book's introduction says that he lived in the City from 1961. In the 1970s he worked a machine that made plastic goods. He spent 10 years with the Kai Fong Association (九龍城砦街坊福利事業促進委員會). He was a volunteer at first, then part-time staff and treasurer. He left a few months before the announcement of the demolition. In 1991, at 75, he still played in the Chiu Chow Music Club. Its members played Chiu Chow (潮州) music.

people.name: Chau Pak
people.story: Chau Pak was a storekeeper in the Walled City. The book names him only in the index of its map. Anna Dalgliesh drew the map in 1992. The index gives no page number for him. The repo has no interview or caption about him. The map shows the City in the late 1980s, at about the time of the clearance announcement. It marks his place as number 5, beside number 29, the Salvation Army Kindergarten. The repo's facts place his store on Lung Chun Back Road, but that is a guess from the map. The book says that the map is not entirely accurate. The sources give nothing about his home, his family or his years in the City.

people.name: Jetly Chau Sau Yee
people.story: Jetly Chau Sau Yee was born in Chiu Chow (潮州) and came to Hong Kong at six. In 1968, at 14, he left school to help his father in the family bakery. Their first shop, on Tung Tau Tsuen Road (東頭村道) in Wong Tai Sin (黃大仙), was demolished. A friend then told them about a new building in the Walled City. The Kai Fong Association (九龍城砦街坊福利事業促進委員會) prepared the purchase agreement for a fee of $200. The family bought the shop before they heard of any plan to demolish the City. The shop was on Sai Shing (West City) Road (西城路), and he called it the cleanest alley. He paid $100 a month for well-water. The shop made several hundred steamed and baked cakes a day for shops, temples, noodle shops and Chiu Chow families. At New Year they worked for several days without a stop. After the clearance was announced in 1987, foreign tour groups often stopped at the shop. He worried about the clearance because a new shop outside the City had to meet licence standards.

people.name: Lau Yeung Yin
people.story: Lau Yeung Yin was born in the Walled City, one of 12 children. His father ran a weaving factory on Lung Chun Back Road (龍津後街). The family lived in the factory. There were no beds, so they moved the yarn aside to make space to sleep. In the early 1960s his father was treasurer of the Kai Fong Association (九龍城砦街坊福利事業促進委員會). Lau left school before the Middle Three examinations. He worked as a tailor's apprentice, then in a rattan shop on Hong Kong Island. Later he worked in his father's factory, which made fabric for gloves. In 1982 he took over the family business in a small factory on Sai Shing (West City) Road (西城路). His sister lent him the money for it. Six people worked there, his wife among them. Business slowed in 1985 and 1986, because customers took their orders to mainland China. The family had a public housing unit in Tai Po but rarely slept there. He expected about $103,000 in compensation for the factory.

people.name: Ng Kam Mui
people.story: Ng Kam Mui's parents moved from Hong Kong Island to the Walled City in the 1960s and opened a café. Her mother was Chiu Chow (潮州). Ng lived or worked at the Chung Fat Café on Tung Tau Tsuen Road (東頭村道) for nearly 30 years. As a child she fetched water from taps at each end of the street and bathed there. After primary school she lived and worked in the City. Her father died young, and her mother fought hard to keep the café. In the 1970s the old building came down, and an 11-storey building went up. The family got two storeys in it and about $7000 for nine months of closure. The café sold tea, coffee, congee and rice from 9 a.m. until late at night. Taxi drivers often came there. She rarely went into the inner City and stayed on its outer edge, where the café was. Later she worked elsewhere in Hong Kong. She asked the Government for $5 million in compensation to buy her mother a flat. The café closed in 1991.

people.name: Lee Yu Chun
people.story: Lee Yu Chun worked in her family's candy business from its start in 1964, when she was not yet 10. Her father started the business, called Chui Fung, in Sham Shui Po. The family later moved to Tsz Wan Shan. In 1967 her father found premises in the Walled City. The family rented two floors of a cottage there but still lived in Tsz Wan Shan. Lee later came to live in the City as well. In the early 1970s the factory moved to 12 Sai Shing (West City) Road (西城路). The family rented it at first and later bought it for $40,000. Lee, her two brothers and her 70-year-old grandmother shared the work. Neighbourhood teenagers wrapped the sweets for 40 cents a pound. Lee's own children helped in the alley after school. Work started at 7 a.m., and the wrapping went on until 9 p.m. About ten years before the interview, she also worked in an electronics factory. She hoped to set up the factory again outside the City after the clearance.

people.name: Law Yu Yi
people.story: Law Yu Yi came from Guangdong. The photo caption calls her a former housewife, and the book's map key calls her a retired maid. At the age of 90 she had lived in the City for 28 years. She lived in a small third-floor flat off Lung Chun First Alley. The flat had no windows and was very humid. She shared it with her daughter-in-law, aged 68. The husbands of both women had died. A surviving son lived on a lower floor of the same building. Each day she went to the adjoining park. There she groomed her face carefully in the traditional Chinese way. She also went to the Old People's Centre (老人中心) to drink tea and meet friends.

people.name: Chan Pui Yin
people.story: Chan Pui Yin came to Hong Kong from Chiu Chow (潮州) county in 1947. He first worked for a pottery distributor on Hong Kong Island. In 1955, at the age of 29, he borrowed money and opened a herbal medicine store on Lung Chun Road (龍津道). Business was good, and he bought the place. Later the two-storey building became an 11-storey block. He got two units for the one that he gave up. He sold mainly herbs and also gave medical consultations. His father, a herbal doctor, taught him. His clients came from all over, some from Hong Kong Island. The shop had Chinese medicines on one side and Western toiletries on the other. It opened from 8am to 11pm, but people knocked on his door at night for medicine. He lived high up in the City, with a view of the sea and fresh air. His three sons and a daughter grew up in the City and kept away from drugs.

people.name: Chan Kwong
people.story: Chan Kwong came from Shantou in Chiu Chow (潮州). He came to Hong Kong with his brother in 1948, at the age of 26. He worked as a hawker and in a plastics factory. In 1970 he opened his own factory, Tai Kwong Plastic Factory, in rented premises on Shing Ngam Road in Kowloon City (九龍城). In 1972 he moved it to Tai Chang Street (大井街) in the Walled City. He made hair clips, toys, ornaments and plastic flowers, and then golf balls. First he employed five or six men. Later he used automatic machines, at times 24 hours a day. At one time, 30 or more women worked for him from home. He sold golf balls to the USA, Japan, France and other countries. The 1970s were his best years. In the City he had fewer inspectors and more freedom. At 67 he planned to retire and go back to the mainland. His son and daughter did not want the business.

people.name: Lee Pui Yuen
people.story: Lee Pui Yuen was a fisherman from Haifeng county. In 1964 he came to Hong Kong by boat with about 10 others. The police held them for three days, but a Christian organisation helped him get out. After a few months in Sham Shui Po, he moved into the Walled City to be with his sister and her family. Four families, more than 20 people, shared about 300 square feet. He had no proper bed space. He worked night shifts in a weaving factory and then had many other jobs. In 1979 he paid about $16,000 to take over a store at 12 Tai Chang Street (大井街). The store had about 700 square feet and sold rice, kerosene, cigarettes and other basic goods. He carried rice and kerosene up 10 or more storeys to customers. The store opened from 8am to midnight. His wife helped him every day. He, his wife and their young son slept behind a partition at the back. The family moved out in 1991.
people.lived: 1964-1991: about 15 years in the City before 1979, then 12 years at his store
people.home: from 1979, a small living area behind a partition at the back of his store, 12 Tai Chang Street (大井街); before that, a very small shared place in the City (four families in about 300 square feet)

people.name: Chung Lo Ying
people.story: Chung Lo Ying and her family first lived in Hung Hom. Robbers scared them there, and in 1958 they moved into the Walled City. They agreed with a Chiu Chow (潮州) family, whose wooden hut had burnt down, to build a house on that family's land. The Chungs paid for the building and took the first floor. That place soon became too small, so they rented another first-floor flat. After about 10 years they bought it. Then a construction company offered them a flat in its new building in exchange. She signed the deal at a tea house, without a lawyer. She bought an apartment on the fourth floor of 82 Lung Chun Road (龍津道), overlooking the park. She first rented it for $80 a month and later paid about $40,000 for it. She had 10 children, and six of them arrived after the move into the City. Her children often joined her for dinner. She rarely locked the door. She did not want the City demolished.
people.lived: from 1958 to at least the time of the interview (more than 30 years); more than 10 years in the 4/F flat

people.name: Chung Yuk Yee
people.story: Chung Yuk Yee was a daughter of Chung Lo Ying. She was born in the Walled City in 1961 and lived there until the clearance in 1991. As a girl she walked the bigger alleys past little houses and working wells. Once she went to a big temple with her mother. The City had no real drains, so every morning the family went to the public lavatories at Tung Tau village (東頭村). Later she married. She lived with her husband, son and daughter in her mother's building, but on the north side. Their flat had no windows, fresh air or view. It was only 230 square feet, with a thin wooden partition between two rooms. All four slept in the bedroom. Family and friends played mahjong in the living room. She helped with the cooking at her mother's flat. She bathed her children in murky water from a rooftop tank. Once a rat ran over her baby daughter's bed.
people.lived: 1961-1991: born in the City; moved out during the clearance in 1991

people.name: Cheng San
people.story: Cheng San was a seaman. At the end of 1967, at about 40, he came back to live in Hong Kong, on the Ngau Tau Kok housing estate. He had six children. He knew no trade, so on a relative's advice he started to make rulers. He first rented a factory on Ko Shan Road. In 1968 he moved to bigger, cheaper premises of about 600 square feet on Tai Chang Street (大井街) in the Walled City. He sawed wood from Borneo by machine and painted the rulers. His daughter printed the measurements upstairs. He once had seven or eight workers and sold to Singapore and Malaysia. Later he worked alone, mostly for local and Macau buyers. He often worked from about 10am until midnight or later. He slept in the factory every night to keep drug addicts from stealing. His wife delivered rulers, and his sons carried the wood. He joined a local association that objected to low compensation. He moved out in 1990.

people.name: Hui Tung Choy
people.story: Hui Tung Choy came to Hong Kong in 1947 to live with his aunt. He was 16, and his parents had died. He grew up in Sun Hui, Guangdong, and had only primary schooling. He learned noodle making with his cousin. Then he opened his own noodle-making place with a friend. His noodle factory at the back of 2 Kwong Ming Street (光明街) opened in 1965. The room was barely 200 square feet and had no windows. Air came in only through the narrow door to the street. He chose the City because rents were low and he needed no licence. At its height in 1980, the business had five workers and made about 1000 noodle discs a day. Later his partner became ill and left, and Hui worked alone. The family owned a flat higher up in the same building. But they cooked and showered in the factory. His two daughters did their homework on the flour-covered work bench. In 1992 he was married with two young daughters. He saw more rats and cockroaches as neighbours moved away.

people.name: Chan Hip Ping
people.story: Chan Hip Ping worked for the Kowloon Walled City Kai Fong Association (九龍城寨街坊福利會). The Association started on 1 May 1963 to serve the residents. As a very young man, Chan boiled water and served at its receptions. From 1966 he was its Vice-President. The Association had its offices on the third floor of 16 Tung Tau Tsuen Road (東頭村道). It cleaned alleys and drains, removed garbage and worked against fires and burglaries. In the 1970s it started to put up road signs and public lights. Later it paid for more than 200 lights. It ran a school from 1968 to 1979. It also took elderly residents on tours, for example to Aberdeen in 1987. The demolition began on 14 January 1987. The Association then called emergency meetings and took the residents' demands to the Government. More than 3000 residents came to its office. At the peak it held nine meetings a day. At the time of the interview, Chan no longer lived in the City. But he still spoke for its community.

people.name: Law Kim Kwong
people.story: Law Kim Kwong was a baker in the Walled City. He made steamed sweet cakes. The book shows his workshop full of cakes in small bowls, beside sacks of flour. Another photograph shows him with crossed arms beside a lit stove. Once he worked through the night to finish cakes for a Chiu Chow (潮州) festival. He had lived in the City for 20 years. He came from the Chiu Chow area of eastern Guangdong. The Chiu Chow people had their own dialect and culture, different from the Cantonese. They made up more than 70 per cent of the City's population. Chiu Chow settlers squatted in and around the City in the late 1940s. Refugees from the same area followed in the early 1950s. The book gives no interview with Law, only photographs and a caption.

people.name: Tsin Mu Lam
people.story: Tsin Mu Lam was a China-trained doctor. His father was a traditional herbal doctor in the City in the 1950s and 1960s. Tsin graduated from the Zhongsan Medical School in Guangzhou in 1961 and practised in China. During the Cultural Revolution, in 1969, he was sent down to the countryside near Dongguan for three years. He came back to Hong Kong in 1973. That year he opened his clinic on the second floor of 10 Tung Tau Tsuen Road (東頭村道). He lived there with his wife and son. He had no Commonwealth qualification, so he was unable to practise outside the City. He used both Chinese and Western medicine. He treated about 30 patients a day, mostly from outside the City. He charged $30 to $40, about a third less than doctors on the housing estates. He bought the clinic outright. He was in his 50s at the interview. For the demolition, more than 80 doctors and dentists elected him to a Government sub-committee. After a hard fight, each clinic was to get $340,000. His clinic closed in 1992.

people.name: Chan Wai Shui
people.story: Chan Wai Shui came to Hong Kong from China in 1947, at the age of 18. He learned the noodle business from his uncle. His old premises in Wang Tau Hom were demolished for the MTR. Thus in 1979 he bought a factory on Lo Yan Street (老人街) for $200,000. Prices outside the Walled City were too high for his small business. He registered the purchase with the Welfare Association and needed no licences. At first there was no electricity, so he arranged for cables. Four partners from before the move worked there about nine hours a day from 8am. His co-workers included Mr Shum and Kwan Tsin On. They made egg noodles and won tun pastry from about 10 bags of flour a day. They delivered by car every day to 40 or 50 regular customers. Chan did not live in the City and seldom slept in the factory. He came only to earn a living. He ran the factory for more than 10 years. He was not sure that the compensation was enough for a new factory.

people.name: Wong Hoi Ming
people.story: Wong Hoi Ming was born in 1920 in the Chiu Chow (潮州) region of Guangdong Province. He learned medicine and kung fu in Thailand and later studied under masters in Chiu Chow. In 1949 he fled to Hong Kong alone and left his wife and family in China. He practised medicine on Hong Kong Island. When his building there was demolished, he moved to the Walled City. He knew the City already because he taught martial arts there. He lived and saw patients in one small apartment with no sunlight. The rent was first $150 a month; later he bought the place. He treated rheumatism, fight injuries and back problems with heated cups, herbal poultices, massage and hot herbal medicines. He had no fixed fees. For a time he let people play mahjong at two tables in the room. He shared a bathroom outside, cooked his own food, and ate with a friend from upstairs. At the clearance he expected about $140,000 for the flat.

people.name: To Gui Bon
people.story: To Gui Bon was born in 1937. He worked in the rubber business before he moved to the City. He was also once a driver of private cars, and he moved to the City when that work became illegal. For about 25 years he made rubber plungers in a small factory on Lung Chun Back Road (龍津後街). At first the site was a two-storey stone house, and he lived on the floor above the factory. When the stone house came down for a new building, he moved next door for a while. At the time of the interview he lived nearby and went home to eat. He worked long hours, sometimes until 2 or 3 a.m. His press had no safety grill, so he worked with extra care. He also made shuttlecocks and sink stoppers. In the 1980s the business grew and made $20,000 to $30,000 a month. He once had a couple of employees, but only one assistant stayed. After the clearance announcement, his business dropped. He had two young children.

people.name: Cheng Koon Yiu
people.story: Cheng Koon Yiu came to Hong Kong with his family in 1948, at the age of five. The family lived near the Walled City. He went to Chung San, a private school on Lung Chun Road (龍津路) inside the City. At 14 he became an apprentice to a relative who was a dentist. He lived on the first floor above the clinic. After his apprenticeship he worked in a factory and then in a clinic in the New Territories. In 1963 he came back to the City to assist a friend. About four years later he set up his own clinic. Later he rented a room from his teacher, who still practised nearby. Many patients came from outside because prices in the City were lower. He earned about $10,000 a month, and his wife helped him. The rent rose step by step from $450 and reached $2000 in 1987. His family, with two girls and a boy, moved into the clinic and slept on the floor.

people.name: Jackie Pullinger
people.story: Jackie Pullinger was a foreign missionary who worked in the Walled City. She did not live there. Mrs Donnithorne, the wife of Hong Kong's archdeacon, first introduced her to the City. In 1973 she set up 'The Well', a meeting place of the St Stephen's Society. Most of its congregation were drug addicts who wanted to give up heroin. Daily prayer there used healing hands, hymns and open confession to God. The programme claimed considerable success compared with Government programmes. It took her years to win the trust of the addicts and the Triads. Some of her first recruits were Triad members who wanted to stop taking drugs. Local and foreign volunteers helped her, and many stayed for several years. Wong Wai Chung, a former addict, first met her in the 1980s in the Walled City youth centre. Shortly after the clearance announcement, she moved to Mongkok and set up a similar programme there.

details.text: She came to Hong Kong in 1966 and went alone into the Walled City.
She took a teaching job outside the Walled City.
She ran a youth club inside the City, to befriend young Triads.
This Times profile gives 1966 as the year she first went into the City, earlier than the 1973 date of 'The Well' in the repo.
She started a youth club in a tiny room in the City, a place for ping pong and darts.
She ran outside camps and weekly excursions, because most young people of the City never saw the light of day.
The St Stephen's Society 'houses' (homes for addicts who came off drugs) started in the 1970s, when she invited an addict into her home.
She took groups of young people to stay on outlying islands, where those who had come off drugs helped the newcomers.

She and some young people took chicken soup every day to 陳太 (Mrs Chan), a sick widow whose son took drugs; Mrs Chan later cooked and cleaned in Pullinger's home (the source does not say that Mrs Chan lived in the City).

people.name: Yim Kwok Yuen
people.story: Yim Kwok Yuen was a farmer in Guangdong Province. From 1971 he tried almost every year to sneak into Hong Kong. He arrived in 1978, at the age of 35. He trained for some months in a roast-food shop. Then he worked in his uncle's roasting shop in the Walled City. When his younger brother arrived three years later, he started his own roast-meat business. The book dates his cooked-meat factory on Lo Yan Street (老人街) to 1981. In the interview he said that he rented the workshop three years earlier. He and his brother ran the rented, unlicensed workshop and roasted pork, chicken and goose. He started work at 4 a.m. every day. He sold the meat as an unlicensed hawker in Wong Tai Sin (黃大仙) market. At first he shared a 200-square-foot room in the City with seven other single men. Later he bought two flats in one building in the City. He lived in one with his brother and uncle and rented out the other.

people.name: Lam Leung Po
people.story: Lam Leung Po became a partner in a minced-fish factory in 1983. The factory was in an alley off Tai Chang Street (大井街), close to the one Government standpipe in the City. Before that, the business was just outside the City, in the Sai Tau Tsuen (西頭村) squatter village, until the village came down. Lam joined the business after it moved into the City. The shop measured about 480 square feet. Rent in the City was cheaper, and the hygiene rules gave less trouble. Nobody asked for protection money, and no hygiene inspector ever came. The factory made minced fish, eel dumplings and squidballs. It made about 300 catties of minced fish a day. Five full-time workers worked with Lam and his partner, and a few neighbour ladies made dumplings part-time. Most customers came from outside the City. The factory sold minced fish to over 200 shops.

people.name: Lam Tseng Yat
people.story: Lam Tseng Yat was born in China in 1916. At 10 he came to Hong Kong with his father and four brothers. The family first sold groceries near the old market in Kowloon City, then at the new market on Sha Bo Road. The Japanese demolished that market in the War. In 1947 the family bought a small property at 25 Tai Chang Street (大井街) and opened a store. The two-storey stone hut later became a seven-storey building, but the land stayed with the family. The shop sold rice, peanut oil, cigarettes, alcohol and fruit. At one time it was the largest grocery business in the City. He called it a father and son business, and it never paid protection money. He lived in the City with his wife, and all his children were born there. The family lived on the first and fourth floors. When the children moved out, the family sold those flats and he lived in the shop. He refused the clearance offer of $210,000 and asked for a shop for a shop.

people.name: Simon Wong
people.story: Simon Wong was the officer of the Salvation Army (救世軍) responsible for the Walled City. The Salvation Army began work in the City in 1968. A girl of about seven had asked it for a primary school. It rented a flat for a school and a church. The landlord tore down pictures of Jesus, but later he sold the flat to the Army. The primary school closed because its pupils did not qualify for public examinations. The kindergarten on Lung Chun Back Road (龍津後街) continued for many years. Parents paid no formal fee, but they gave $100 a term if they had the money. It looked for sponsors among foreign groups, and one Austrian gentleman sent over $100,000 each year. At least twice a month, the school took the children to a park outside the City or to Kowloon Park. On Sundays the premises became a chapel for 10 to 20 people. Wong said that the City was a peaceful community in the 1960s and 1970s. After the clearance was announced, reports said that crime increased.

people.name: Reverend Isaac Liu
people.story: Isaac Liu was born in 1935. In 1950 he came to Hong Kong from his native village in China. He did not speak Cantonese, and he often felt lonely. A stranger gave him the gospel in Mandarin, and he became a Christian. He volunteered to preach and studied at a seminary for three years. In that time he began work in the Walled City, with a school in a few rented wooden shacks. In 1960 the mission opened a Gospel Centre in a four-storey building on Lung Shing Road (龍城路). It held a chapel, a clinic for drug addicts and the Tak Shing school, which had more than 420 pupils at its peak. In 1971 the mission moved to the old magistrate's buildings, the Yamen (衙門), at the centre of the City. He began to live in the City in the same year. The school closed in 1978, and in 1979 he started the Old People's Centre (老人中心). It grew to 184 members. The clearance forced him to leave the premises in 1991.

details.text: His Chinese name is 劉知三: the CNEC article quotes the Chinese edition of the book (黑暗之城：九龍城寨的日與夜, 中華書局 2015, p314) with his words that he lived in the City from 1971, the same words as Isaac Liu's in the English book.
He said: from the mid-1950s he went in and out of the City often; in the 1960s, from the school roof, he always saw drug addicts squatting in the lanes.
He said that nobody gave him trouble, because people knew that the mission worked for the residents.
In the early years a second CNEC pastor, 張祖鷺, also served in the City; the families of both pastors lived in the City.

The two pastors turned the school into the Old People's Centre because the City had more than 600 old people whose windows could not open and whose flats never saw daylight; the Yamen (恩光園) was the only place in the City with no high building.
At its peak the centre served 187 members (the English book says 184).
The centre opened in 1979 and ran until the clearance; 30 old people were baptised there in that time.
In 1991 the Old People's Centre moved to Fu Shin Estate (富善邨), Tai Po.
The CNEC article puts the 1960 Gospel Centre in a four-storey tenement on Lung Chun Road (龍津道), not on Lung Shing Road (the English book).
In 1956 CNEC opened the 慈光贈診所 (free clinic) on Lung Shing Road (龍城路), with drug-addiction treatment; classes for addicts' children were held upstairs.
The school (德成分校, later 恩光學校) taught kindergarten to Primary 6; most pupils came from the City.
He is one of five preachers whom Kowloon Walled City Park commemorates for their work for the residents (with 鄺日修, 潘靈卓 (Jackie Pullinger) and the Willans couple).
The table of contents of the Chinese edition of the book (黑暗之城──九龍城寨的日與夜, 中華書局) prints the Chinese name 劉知三 beside the English name.

people.name: Kwok Lau Hing
people.story: Kwok Lau Hing never lived in the City itself, but she was a regular visitor to its Old People's Centre (老人中心). In her 30s she and her elder sister left Shanghai Street in Yau Ma Tei. They bought a small flat on the second floor of 5C Sai Tau New Street, a settlement on the outskirts of the City. She owned a half share and rented one of her two rooms out. She worked half days as a cleaner and office woman for the Jardine Airline Company in Central. She earned about $100 a month and assembled toys for extra money. She never dared to go into the Walled City itself. Her husband died and left her with two sons and a daughter. The Government decided to clear the settlement in 1985, and the family moved to the Lok Wah estate. After she retired at 65, she joined the Old People's Centre. There she learnt to write and did handcraft and embroidery. She kept making the journey after she moved to Junk Bay. In 1989 she was 73.

people.name: Yu Hing Wan
people.story: Yu Hing Wan made muslin in the City. Muslin was once a major industry there, before synthetic materials came. At 86 he was still at work, and he was the last muslin maker in the City. Like most factory owners in the City, he chose his site on Lung Chun Road (龍津道) for its cheap rent. He needed space for large machinery and for stored cloth. He felt that outside the City the business was not viable, and that there he was not able to own a factory. He lived in the City for 18 years. He came from the Hakka community of Guangdong province. Thus he was in a minority among the mainly Chiu Chow (潮州) population of the City. His factory was neat and clean. But after long years of hard work, the noise of the old machines and the lack of ventilation hurt him most. The photographs show him at a large machine and with long rolls of white cloth.

people.name: Chan Kwan Leung
people.story: Chan Kwan Leung grew up in the first resettlement estates at Shek Kip Mei, and later in the New Territories. His parents were teachers. At 24 he worked for the Hong Kong Telephone Company and left his parents' house. In 1981 he moved into the Walled City, where he bought a flat for $68,000. He met his wife there. Her mother gave him a pigeon, and soon he kept many birds. In about 1981 or 1982 he built cages on the roof of his building. The owner of the flat below agreed, but other people complained. He quit his job to care for the birds, and at one stage he had more than 1000. He did not tell his wife or his parents. He bought and sold pigeons and started a pigeon-racing club with friends. The club raced birds from Shanghai and other places in China. In January 1987 the Housing Department registered him as a resident and announced the clearance. On that day he decided to close his pigeon business.

people.name: Chu Yiu Shan
people.story: Chu Yiu Shan was born in 1951 and grew up in the Walled City. His parents ran a store. At about 13 he delivered drinks to nearby places, some of them opium, gambling and sex-show dens. Later he became an intermediary between the sellers and buyers of flats, because he had seen much cheating. As a long-time resident, he could find out who the real owners were. He said that his property business became the biggest in the City and earned him about $20,000 a month. He saw water as the main hardship of the residents. He moved to Junk Bay when the clearance was announced. The GRS clearance file of his firm, Hang Fai Property Co., gives his Chinese name as 朱耀山 and the firm's address as 17 Tai Chang Street (大井街).

people.name: Lam Shu Chuen
people.story: Lam Shu Chuen came to the Walled City from the mainland as a small boy, before the War, and lived there for more than 50 years. He said that he once owned land in the City, which he bought for $25. In the 1940s he made his money by renting out kerosene lamps, and later he sold electricity from generators. In 1953 he was the first person in the City to own a car. He was a senior member of the Kai Fong Association (九龍城寨街坊福利會) and for many years chairman of the Industrial Commercial Liaison Committee. His family factory made components for radio-controlled toys. He called the clearance compensation not at all fair. After the clearance he moved the factory to Tai Po.

people.name: Mrs Law
people.story: Mrs Law was a grandmother in the Walled City. Every day she collected her two grandchildren from school and took them back to her small apartment for the afternoon. The children often did their homework on her bed while they knelt on the floor. Their parents, who both worked full-time, picked them up on their way home from work. The book gives her only in a photo caption, and gives no address or dates.

people.name: Lui Man Sang
people.story: Lui Man Sang was the senior postman of the Walled City. The book says that few people knew the layout of the City as completely as he did. He knew its buildings, alleys, staircases and rooftops, also in the building boom of the late 1970s, when addresses changed often. His daily round began at a store on Lo Yan Street (老人街). From there he climbed dark stairwells and crossed the rooftops from building to building. His apprentice, the postman Lam Po Chun (林寶鎮), started with him at 19, when Mr Lui was 32. The two men were nicknamed 'the rooftop posties'. At the end of the 1980s, after about eight years together, Mr Lui moved to a different job.
people.lived: postman in the City from about 1979 to the end of the 1980s (Lam Po Chun's account); the book does not say where he lived

people.name: Chan Shing
people.story: Chan Shing was one of the 70 or so private water suppliers of the Walled City. He collected the monthly charges from his customers himself. Sometimes he waived the charge for the elderly. He said: "we are all poor people here and we should help each other". His pump was usually hidden behind a floor panel. At various times he switched it on to fill a large storage tank on the roof. The book gives him only in a photo caption, with no address or dates.

people.name: Mr Shum
people.story: Mr Shum worked with Chan Wai Shui in his noodle factory on Lo Yan Street (老人街). He made the pastry sheets that became the wrappers of won tun. He had made won tun pastry for years, and before that he made noodles. Every day he made more than 100 pounds of pastry. A machine stirred the flour, but he rubbed it by hand and flattened it with a long pole, on which he sat. He said that the work was hard and that he was often soaked to the skin.
people.lived: worked in the City at the time of the photographs (c.1990); the book gives no years

sources.quote: Since the inception of the Assessment Review Board, one case of appeal against the adequacy of Government's compensation offer has been heard at the request of a Walled City resident.

details.text: Tsang Keong took the compensation offer to the Assessment Review Board of the Housing Authority Special Committee on Clearance of Kowloon Walled City: GRS holds 'Tsang Keong - ARB [Assessment Review Board] Submission' (25.11.1991 - 25.2.1993) and 'Tsang Keong Dental Clinic - ARB [Assessment Review Board] Material' (3.6.1992 - 10.6.1993).
Another file spells the name 'Tsang Keung Dental Practice' (17.12.1992 - 12.5.1993).

The Board was an administrative appeal body set up in 1987; a resident or the Government Land Agent could convene it, and it decided whether an offer was fair. By 4 Dec 1991 only one appeal had been heard, and two more had just been submitted by residents; the Tsang Keong submission file opens on 25 Nov 1991, thus it was probably one of those two.

people.name: Chan Cheung-chuen
people.story: Chan Cheung-chuen (陳祥全) was a tenant in the Walled City with his wife. HK01 says that the couple left a partitioned room in Kowloon City (九龍城) in 1979. In the City, a rent of about HK$800 got them a whole flat. He said that it was at least a space of their own. WSJ gives his years inside as 1985-1991 and a household of three. His first home was Room B, 12/F, 31 Tung Tau Tsuen Road (東頭村道). Later the family rented Room 2, 11/F, 16 Tung Tau Tsuen Road. The rent went from HK$800-900 a month to HK$1,100. As an engineering student, he spent four months on a hand-drawn map of the City. He walked its dark, dripping alleys, none of them wider than three feet. He finished the map in March 1987, two months after the government announced the clearance. He paid little attention to the clearance because he was only a tenant.

details.text: As a child he lived in Tung Tau Estate, outside the City; he first went into the City with classmates to visit a friend who lived there, and played hide and seek in its dark corners.
He moved into the City after he got married, to start his family.
His work related to mechanical drawing; when the City was about to be demolished he drew his own map, of the streets and of the upper-level walkways between buildings.

He said that neighbours swapped ingredients through the windows when they cooked dinner (for example soy sauce), that a shout for help alerted everyone, and that the City was sometimes safer than outside.
He said that many couples in the Kaifong (Neighbourhood Welfare Association) met in the City.
The map is of the City shortly before the demolition (the source gives no date).
He said that he sometimes thought the City was safer than outside.
(Cantonese transcript) He grew up in Tung Tau Estate (東頭邨), not in the City.
(Cantonese transcript) He moved into the City when he married and needed a small home (蝸居).
(Cantonese transcript) Neighbours cooking dinner opened the window and asked each other for soy sauce; they swapped ingredients through the windows often.
(Cantonese transcript) In a fire, neighbours warned each other because they lived so close.
As a boy he went to the City with classmates to visit a friend and played hide-and-seek there.
He mapped the intertwined streets and the upper-level walkways that linked the buildings.
Neighbours borrowed ingredients through the windows ('Hey do you have some soy sauce?').

people.name: Albert Ng Kam-po
people.story: Albert Ng Kam-po (吳錦波) was born in China during the Cultural Revolution. He and his family moved from Chiu Chow (潮州) in southern China to Hong Kong. There they joined his father, a Chinese man born in Thailand. The family lived in the Walled City from 1975 to 1991 or 1992. At once they belonged to the strong Chiu Chow community of the City. The family of five owned Room A, 7/F, 8 Sz Kung Street (社公街). The flat had more than 200 sq ft, and the family bought it in 1975 for about HK$50,000. Albert went to school outside the City. He remembered how he played on its roofs and in its corridors. Later he recalled that he lived on the eighth floor, in a building with no lift. As an adult he became a pastor.

details.text: In 2013, aged 45, he was a pastor at the English-speaking Island Evangelical Community Church in Quarry Bay.
He said the family moved into the Walled City because it was relatively cheaper.
He speaks as a former resident who grew up there in Paul French's BBC Radio 3 documentary 'Return to the City of Darkness' (2026).
He was born in a farming village in Mainland China.
His mother took him and his sister to Hong Kong when he was a young child.
The family lived in the City until it was demolished.
His own blog says that his family moved into the City in the mid-1970s and lived there until the demolition in the early 1990s.
He lived on the 8th floor of a building with no lift.
The family bought rice and LPG gas from a grocery ('rice shop') inside the City owned by the parents of his friend Ah Meng; Ah Meng's older brother Ah Keung delivered them up the stairs.
As a boy he picked up empty soda bottles in the dark alleys and returned them to the grocery for a 20-cent refund each.
Ah Meng's parents, the grocery owners, introduced him to their son Ah Meng (who lived outside the City) so that the boys could play table tennis together.
Later he became a pastor; Island ECC says that he lived in the City for more than ten years and hopes to write a book about it.
He is married to Elisa; they have two sons.
His mother scolded him for collecting the bottles and forbade it.
He bought stamps from an old man outside Kowloon City Christians' Church on Lung Kong Road (outside the City) and resold them to Ah Meng.
He said that every day he walked through the dark alleys while water dripped all the time.
He ended his account of the hard life in the City with: 'But we had hope.'

people.name: Wong Yum-fai
people.story: Wong Yum-fai (王欽輝) made fishballs in the Walled City. Lore said that 80% of the fishballs of Hong Kong came from the City. He supplied fishballs and fishcakes to wholesale markets, and he sold 30 catties (40 pounds) of fishballs a day. Later he opened a noodle shop on the ground floor of his own building. A bowl of fishball noodles cost HK$0.30 to HK$0.80. His family of eight lived in the same building, on 8/F, 33 Lo Yan Street (老人街). The flat had 500 sq ft. When his children were old enough, they helped in the family business. His son Wong Chun-ping (王鎮平) was one of them. The WSJ fact box gives the years of the family inside as 1972-1983. The WSJ video says that he lived in the City for 30 years.

They lived on 8/F, 33 Lo Yan Street (老人街), in a flat of 500 sq ft. The source gives their years inside as 1972-1983. His father supplied fishballs and fishcakes to wholesale markets, about 30 catties a day. Later his father opened a noodle shop on the ground floor of the same building. When the children were old enough, they helped in the family business. The source does not give his age or his tasks.

people.name: Yeung Lai-wan
people.story: Yeung Lai-wan (楊麗雲) was a mother of nine. She lived in the Walled City from 1959 to 1981. Her husband was a chef, but he lost his job after the stock-market crash of 1973. Then the couple became hawkers. They sold dim sum from a wooden street cart outside the City. In the 1970s, siu mai cost HK$0.10 and a bao HK$0.80. The family income was HK$6,000 to HK$7,000 a month. WSJ gives three homes in the City. They were 2/F, Sai Shing Road (西城路) and 3/F, 60 Lung Chun Road (龍津道). The third was 4/F, Fu Hing House (富興樓), Lung Chun Road. The flats had 200, 600 and 500 sq ft. In 1974 the family bought a flat for HK$10,000. She once saw a heroin addict dig out the eye of a cat and eat it. The poor air in the home harmed her health. Thus the family moved away.
people.home: 2/F, Sai Shing Rd. (Chinese fact box: 西城路2号2楼); 3/F, 60 Lung Chun Rd.; 4/F, Lung Chun Rd. (Chinese fact box: 龙津路富兴楼4楼)

people.name: Paul Tang Kam-cheung
people.story: Paul Tang Kam-cheung (鄧金祥) lived in the Walled City from 1948 to 1979. His family of seven lived on the ground floor in Lung Chun Road 2nd Lane (龍津二巷). The home had 400 to 500 sq ft, and the family earned HK$8 to HK$10 a day. In the 1950s, as a teenager, he joined the Hong Fat Shan (洪發山) triad, later called the 14K. The gang dealt in drugs and ran illegal gambling, strip clubs and brothels. He gave the protection money of 1959-1962 as HK$5 a day. Tang became a heroin addict. He went to jail for robbery and for drugs. He said that the police patrolled at set hours but did not stay long. Triad knife fights took place off the main streets. Later he became a Christian and a pastor. Then he moved out of the City.

people.name: Lam Po-chun
people.story: Lam Po-chun (林寶鎮) was a postman in the Walled City. He started to deliver mail there at the age of 18. He worked inside from 1979 to 1991. Only one other postman served the area. This man was his mentor, and he recruited Lam. He chose Lam for his 'naughty boy' personality. This nature let Lam think flexibly. The chaotic house numbers of the City asked for this skill. His daily shift was eight hours. WSJ gave an estimate of 350 buildings in the City. Only two of them had lifts. The source does not say where he lived.

people.name: Wong Chan Pui-wah
people.story: Wong Chan Pui-wah (黃陳佩華) was a garment-factory worker. WSJ quoted her in the Explore chapter of its 2014 interactive. She remembered the Salvation Army (救世軍) school inside the Walled City. The Salvation Army ran a primary school there, and later a kindergarten. She said that many children went to school there. The children played together and sang songs. She called it very happy and very different from the schools of today. WSJ credits her for a photo of the kindergarten. She spoke about electric power too. She said that they paid somebody to 'steal' electricity for them. WSJ also names her as the source of its dim sum prices of 1971. The source does not give her years in the City or her address.

people.name: 芬姐
people.story: 芬姐 grew up in the Walled City. HK01 met her in 2016 with four other former residents. Her family had a small store (士多) in the City. When her mother went to carry water, 芬姐 minded the store alone. Many young men came to buy, and sales went up. She met her sweetheart in the City and settled there. She did not see the City as a 'city of sin'. She said that people born there were used to the vice. On 14 January 1987 she was in a hair salon inside the City. She was getting a perm before a festival. A customer told her that the government had sealed the City. Then the radio gave the news. At home, officials told the family to register, and they registered. She was proud to come from the City.

people.name: Mr Lau
people.story: Mr Lau (劉先生) was 73 in 2016. He lived in the Walled City from the age of six. His first home there was a tin hut. In those years the City had mostly low stone houses and tin huts. A volunteer night watch patrolled and called out warnings about fire. Later the demand for homes grew. Businessmen bought land from residents and put up high-rises of ten or more storeys. The builders took his tin hut, and he got a flat in the new building. He had no land deed and paid no rates or land tax. A paper with the buyer, seller, date and price was the only record. The residents' welfare association witnessed it and stamped it. The Lau family lived on the sixth floor. A friend who visited saw rats, dirty water and leaking pipes. Lau stayed until the clearance, when he was 47. He said that the residents had hoped for the clearance for some time.

people.name: Mrs Lau
people.story: Mrs Lau (劉太) moved into the Walled City as an adult. At first she was not used to it and often got lost. In time she got used to the poor conditions. She said that nothing there scared her. She found the City stable and safe. The vice trades did not bother residents for no reason. She told how the Lau family escaped a fire. The family lived on the sixth floor, and a rattan shop below caught fire. The back stair was locked. The family went down to the third floor, which faced the corridor of the next building. They handed their newborn baby to a neighbour across the gap. Then they stepped across. She laughed that it was not frightening at all. On 14 January 1987 she came home from the market and saw crowds outside the City. By the clearance her children were grown, and she wanted a change of surroundings.

people.name: 林羅平
people.story: 林羅平 (HK01 calls him 平哥) made fishballs in the Walled City, but he did not live there. As a boy he came from Chiu Chow (潮州) with his parents and his brother. The family settled in Lok Fu (樂富). His brother made fishballs from the age of nine. When 林羅平 was in Primary 3, his brother rented a small ground-floor shop in the City as a fishball workshop. After school 林羅平 helped there. They had no machines, so they scraped the fish by hand. He got home at about 9 or 10 p.m. In 1983, at 24, he opened his own wholesale shop in the City with HK$6,000. The landlord came from his home area and gave him a low rent. He needed no licence and paid no tax. His shop was near the outer street and had a meter from the power company. The police signed a patrol book outside his shop. He never paid protection money. After the clearance he kept the business. In 2024 he still ran 德興魚蛋 in Kowloon City (九龍城).

details.text: In June 2026 he was 67 and said that he had made fishballs from the age of 15, for more than half a century.
He works in the shop 364 days a year and rests only on the first day of the Lunar New Year (大年初一).
He uses eel (黃鱔) and 滑仔魚 for the fishballs, and a fish-paste machine (啤魚肉機) more than 50 years old.
The machine that he still uses to make fishballs is the one that he moved out of the City.
If the machine is the same one, it was in his workshop in the City in December 1986.
He was born in about 1959 (67 in June 2026); that fits HK01's age of 24 in 1983.
English-language sources call him Uncle Ping, Lam Lo-ping or Lam Law-ping, owner of Tak Hing (德興) fishballs; the business began as a wholesale factory deep inside the City.
He wakes at 5 a.m. every day to prepare fish glue (a mixture of ice and fish paste).
He told this source that he started as a teenager by helping at a street stall (HK01 says it was his brother's rented workshop in the City).
When the City was demolished many street vendors moved to the Mainland, but he stayed in Hong Kong.
If he kept the same hours in 1986, he started work at about 5 a.m.
His wife (林太太) has complained about his long hours.
He came from Chiu Chow (潮州) in his teens with his parents and elder brother, lived around Lok Fu (樂富), and in the 1980s opened a fishball workshop in the City.
He was just over 20 when he opened, renting a shop with HK$6,000 of capital, thanks to the City's 'three no-cares' status.
His workshop was on Kwong Ming Street (光明街), which had several fishball workshops and also pig-blood, plastic-flower and garment workshops.
Shop rent plus water and electricity came to under HK$2,000 a month.
Many workshops were family workshops with no money for hired hands; all the staff were family members.
Police patrolled the City's main streets two or three times every day.
He felt the City was very peaceful and saw no triad bullying.
Neighbours greeted each other all day long.
After the clearance he joined his elder brother, also a fishball-workshop owner, and moved to Fuk Lo Tsun Road (福佬村道), Kowloon City.
Today he runs 德興魚蛋公司 with his wife May姐 on Fuk Lo Tsun Road.

people.name: 阿榮
people.story: 阿榮 is a pseudonym that HK01 gave to a man in his sixties in 2016. His parents came from mainland China in the early 1950s. They were poor, and the Walled City had the lowest rents in Hong Kong. He lived in the City from his birth to the age of 20. HK01 gives his home as 西頭村第一街, and puts his door on 成龍街. The home had no proper water or power. Ten or more homes shared one wire, and fires broke out at night. The wells gave water only for a few hours each afternoon. Heroin sellers had stalls in the back lane at his door. His parents sent him to a primary school outside, in Kowloon City (九龍城). He did not play in the City. He did not join a triad and did not take drugs. For many years he did not tell his daughter about his childhood.
people.lived: from his birth (his parents came in the early 1950s) to the age of 20
people.home: 西頭村第一街; the same article puts his door on 成龍街

people.name: Yip Tak-wai
people.story: Yip Tak-wai (葉德偉) bought a 400 sq ft flat inside the Walled City in 1976. He paid HK$30,000. On 14 January 1987 he was at work in an office in Central (中環). He heard on the radio that the government had sealed the City, and he was shocked. He explained the surprise: the government did not want new people to move in for compensation. He said that vice was in Lung Shing Road (龍城路) and Kwong Ming Street (光明街). Sai Tau Tsuen (西頭村), outside the City, also had brothels and drugs. He remembered many scholars with fine calligraphy, several school bodies and only one martial-arts school. He and the four other HK01 residents agreed to move out at the clearance. Later they formed a residents' welfare association (九龍城寨街坊福利會), and Yip became its general secretary. He said that the City was a self-governing community.

people.name: Lam Yin Ming
people.story: Lam Yin Ming was one of the last residents of the Walled City. In June 1992 about 100 holdouts remained from more than 30,000 residents. Lam was one of the resisters. He led a reporter inside the City. They went down a long dark corridor and around several corners. Then they climbed about six flights of stairs. They passed big spider webs, strong smells, rats and a few one-man workshops. At the top was the door of his two-room flat. The authorities had locked it months before. Lam tried to push a finger through a small hole in the door. He said that the flat was his home and a good place to live. He and a few dozen others planned to fight the eviction on 1 July 1992.

people.name: Wang Ching
people.story: Wang Ching was the 41-year-old owner of a plastic factory. In June 1992 she was one of the last holdouts of the Walled City. About 100 of the more than 30,000 residents remained. The government had paid compensation and moved many people to public housing. A small group refused to leave. They camped in a roadside shelter by one of the few unlocked entrances. They wanted more money. They also cited the treaty of 1898 between Britain and China, which disallowed the expulsion of the residents. Wang Ching pointed to a large portrait of Mao on a nearby wall. She said that the place was China, not Hong Kong. She said that the British government had no power to move them. The police planned to come with eviction orders the next day.

people.name: Liu Ziqun
people.story: Liu Ziqun worked in the Walled City. On 7 August 1983 Xu Jiatun, director of the Hong Kong branch of Xinhua, visited the Walled City and met him in the Self-Rule Organization Office, up a narrow staircase. His office was a room of slightly more than 10 square metres. Xu described him as young and capable; he greeted the visitors warmly. He said that the residents were fairly united, but their living conditions were poor; drinking water was a particular problem. He said that many residents who had fled from the mainland were afraid of punishment after 1997.

details.text: On 7 August 1983 Xu Jiatun, director of the Hong Kong branch of Xinhua, visited the Walled City and met him in the Self-Rule Organization Office, up a narrow staircase.
His office was a room of slightly more than 10 square metres.
Xu described him as young and capable; he greeted the visitors warmly.
He said that the residents were fairly united, but their living conditions were poor; drinking water was a particular problem.
He said that many residents who had fled from the mainland were afraid of punishment after 1997.

The romanization 'Liu Ziqun' is the JPRS (Mandarin pinyin) spelling; the source gives no characters and no Cantonese spelling. The 'Self-Rule Organization Office' is probably the translator's name for a residents' body such as the Kaifong association, but the source does not say so.
'worked daily' is my inference from his post as secretary of an office inside the City; the source does not say how often he was there or whether he lived in the City.

people.name: Louisa Wong
people.story: Louisa Wong lived in the Walled City. Born on 21 September 1957. The family lived in one small room of about 100 sq ft. The monthly rent was HK$30. Prostitutes lived in the room on one side and heroin addicts on the other. Her parents fled Communist China in the 1940s. Her parents struggled to feed a family that grew to six children. Dinner was often steamed rice with melted pig fat and soy sauce. She remembers the place as very dark, very smelly, sweaty and chaotic. The family left when her parents won a lottery for subsidised public housing. She later founded the first home-grown headhunting firm in China (1996) and became executive chairman of Global Sage; she was 'born to a refugee family' in the Walled City. She speaks as a former resident in the BBC Radio 3 documentary 'Return to the City of Darkness' (2026), with Paul French. The rent in the new public housing estate was HK$90 a month. After the move to the public housing flat (rent HK$90), instead of going to nursery school she worked with her sister and aunt in a plastic-flower factory to help with the rent; the work made her fingers bleed. She was five.

people.name: Heung Yin-king
people.story: Heung Yin-king lived in the Walled City. In the 1960s the Heung family of six moved from a rooftop hut in Hung Hom to the Walled City. First home: a 70 sq ft room in a two-storey house near Tung Tau Chuen Road, shared with seven other families. The family ate from a board laid over the knitting machine and sat on the bed; there was no space for a dinner table. She says the family had the best times in the first house. Several years later they moved to a two-bedroom flat on the fourth floor of a high-rise on Tai Cheng Street. The second home had no taps; as the eldest daughter she hauled buckets of water from the public taps up four floors to the flat every day. 'Life was poor, but we were very happy.'

people.name: Ida Shum
people.story: Ida Shum lived in the Walled City. A former resident, 62 in 2013, later living in Hung Hom. Her neighbour always helped her take care of her children, and they cooked for each other. The neighbour's help let her focus on her work and earn money to feed her family. 'We all had very good relationships in very bad conditions.' 'People who lived there were always loyal to each other.' Flood: water rose to people's knees with rubbish floating, and residents walked through it barefoot. She still kept in touch with old neighbours, some of whom were overseas. 'In the Walled City, the sunshine always followed the rain.' She said the City was a haven for triad groups such as the 14K and Sun Yee On, who jealously controlled their territory.

people.name: Lau Chun-fat
people.story: Lau Chun-fat lived in the Walled City. 83 in 2018 (born about 1935). He came to Hong Kong from Fujian in 1974. At a toy factory, his boss told him about cheap homes in the Walled City. He bought a flat for his family in the late 1980s for around HK$40,000. Water: the family drew buckets of drinking and cooking water from a nearby public tap. He felt safe: hooligans did not dare to come in because it was not their neighbourhood. He saw no building collapse and no fires. At the clearance he wanted to stay but accepted about HK$120,000 compensation, and bought another flat in a nearby tenement building, where he lived in 2018 with his wife, a son and a daughter.

people.name: Vivian Chan
people.story: Vivian Chan lived in the Walled City. A US-based family physician in her 40s (2018); she spent more than 10 years in the City in her childhood and adolescence. Home: a 600 sq ft flat on the 10th floor of a cramped building. In 2018 she lived in a two-storey house with a small garage in America. She often came across junkies who slept under the stairs. As a primary-school child she was held at knifepoint for money by a young junkie; she burst into tears and he ran. Neighbours told her stories of who was beaten up, who took drugs and who was assaulted. She does not miss the place ('unhygienic, dirty and seedy') but says it had a unique culture. She went back once and found the park 'really clean and rejuvenating'. For her the Walled City is 'a distant unwelcomed memory'.

people.name: Gordon Lam Ka-tung
people.story: Gordon Lam Ka-tung (林家棟), later a film actor, moved into the Walled City with his family before he was 10 and lived there for four years. He was born in 1967 on South Wall Road (城南道), next to the City; his father traded jade. The family lived on the 12th floor of a building with no lift. Every day after school he took a red plastic bucket to the street corner and queued for water. He often bought egg tarts at a cha chaan teng on Lung Chun Road (龍津道).

people.name: Ha Fan-ming
people.story: Ha Fan-ming (夏藩銘) lived and worked in the Walled City. In 1968 he and his wife took over a noodle stall opposite Wong Tai Sin police station; they used their home as a workshop. The next year they moved into the City and went on making cuttlefish balls at home, mainly for wholesale to Chiu Chow restaurants. In the 1960s he and his wife lived in the City and used the home as a workshop for cuttlefish balls and pork balls. Later the noodle shop moved to Yau Ma Tei; the couple cut fish, beat the paste and piped fishballs every day for more than 40 years. His eldest son Roger reopened Ha Ming Kee in Sai Ying Pun in 2018. He and his wife Chan So-hing founded Ha Ming Kee in the narrow alleys of the City (SCMP). He and his wife came from Chiu Chow (潮州) to Hong Kong in the 1960s and started to sell fishballs out of necessity. The family did not leave the City until the demolition began in 1993. He made the deliveries by bicycle while his wife made the fishballs at home. The family lived on the eighth floor, with no lift. At its height Ha Ming Kee supplied 70 per cent of the restaurants in the Yau Tsim Mong district. All his children graduated from universities overseas. In 1983 his wife took over a noodle shop on Victory Road, Ho Man Tin (何文田勝利道), and founded Ha Ming Kee (夏銘記麵家).

people.name: Chan So-hing
people.story: Chan So-hing (陳素卿) lived and worked in the Walled City. She and her husband Ha Fan-ming founded Ha Ming Kee; it was a husband-and-wife business. In 1983 she took over a noodle shop on Victory Road, Ho Man Tin, and founded Ha Ming Kee. She made the fishballs at home while her husband delivered them by bicycle. Her son remembers her cleaning the fish at the pump in the street. She gutted and cleaned all the fish at the pump, in cold water, because the flat had no room for that work. people.name: Roger Ha
people.story: Roger Ha lived in the Walled City. He is the eldest son of Ha Fan-ming (夏藩銘); he reopened Ha Ming Kee in Sai Ying Pun in 2018. He came back to Hong Kong in 2012 to help his parents when his mother had heart disease. He grew up on the eighth floor of a building in the City with no lift. people.name: Winson
people.story: By about 1970 Winson lived in the Walled City. He was an opium addict and a leader in one of its triad gangs, and he controlled its fights with other gangs over turf. His gang leader, Goko, sent him to guard Jackie Pullinger's youth club. She did not want gang protection, but he came every night. At first he waited outside; then he began to pray with the club. After half an hour of prayer he came off opium and never went back. He stayed beside Pullinger and went with her on her mission work in the City.

details.text: In the 1980s he and a friend jointly bought a ~200 sq ft flat in the City for over HK$140,000; the friend lived with him.

At the clearance the friend wanted the cash compensation, and his restaurant job gave him a dormitory, so the two chose compensation; together they got HK$150,000, so he got only HK$75,000 and lived in the restaurant dormitory.
He gave up public housing for the compensation, did not use the money to buy a Home Ownership flat, and rented a subdivided flat in Jordan (佐敦).

Later he was a security guard and then a gardener; after losing the gardener job he became homeless. In 2023, aged 74, he filed a judicial review because the Housing Authority refused his public-housing applications on the ground of the Walled City compensation.
He was a former Walled City resident, aged 74 in 2023, surnamed Hui.
In the 1980s he co-owned a 250 sq ft flat with a friend. In 1993 he accepted HK$70,000 compensation for its demolition; he and the friend split the HK$140,000 offer.

Because he took cash instead of a public flat, the Housing Authority rejected his public-housing applications four times. In 2023 he lived on CSSA in a transitional housing flat and applied for judicial review.

people.name: 阿平
people.story: 阿平 worked in the summers in the Walled City. Every summer from Primary 4 to the summer of Form 1 he went into the City to work for his aunt (伯娘), who ran a plastic factory moulding toys. He entered the City from Tung Tau Tsuen Road through a very narrow lane, Kwong Ming Street (光明街). He went in each time with his elder sister, winding through the City to the factory. The buildings were nearly all connected: the stair to the factory also led into the next building's lobby. His first impression was noise: the moulding machines never stopped and he had to cover his ears. The moulding was downstairs; he worked upstairs tearing gun cases and parts of plastic dolls and toy guns from the moulds (搣水口). Each summer there were four or five wire fires (燒電線); at the shout everyone ran out to the Tung Tau Tsuen Road entrance. He spent four summers in the factory. In 1979 the factory moved from the City to Huizhou (惠州), and he never went back.

details.text: Every summer from Primary 4 to the summer of Form 1 he went into the City to work for his aunt (伯娘), who ran a plastic factory moulding toys.
He entered the City from Tung Tau Tsuen Road through a very narrow lane, Kwong Ming Street (光明街).
He went in each time with his elder sister, winding through the City to the factory.
The buildings were nearly all connected: the stair to the factory also led into the next building's lobby.
His first impression was noise: the moulding machines never stopped and he had to cover his ears.
The moulding was downstairs; he worked upstairs tearing gun cases and parts of plastic dolls and toy guns from the moulds (搣水口).
Each summer there were four or five wire fires (燒電線); at the shout everyone ran out to the Tung Tau Tsuen Road entrance.
He spent four summers in the factory.
In 1979 the factory moved from the City to Huizhou (惠州), and he never went back.

people.name: 阿平's elder brother
people.story: 阿平's elder brother went to school in the Walled City. Their father, a strong patriot, moved him from an outside school into a primary school in the City; he thought the City's schoolboys were better behaved, all with shaved heads. A group of pupils from Wang Tau Hom and Tung Tau Tsuen walked into the City for school; he studied there only one year before his mother took him out. The school was strongly patriotic but weak academically; with the secondary-entrance exam coming, his mother moved him. The school was 城寨坊眾學校; pupils wore white shirts and blue shorts. Patriots from the mainland founded it; the teachers had taught on the mainland and had no Hong Kong teaching licence. The school closed in 1979; some teachers tried for years to get severance pay.

people.work: a pupil of the 城寨坊眾學校, a primary school in the City

people.name: 陳慎芝
people.story: 陳慎芝 worked in the Walled City. Inside the City there were hundreds of men divided among triad societies (字頭); each shed (棚) was a unit, and he ran the first row as its 棚主. A boss (話事人) then also paid him HK$30 a day to patrol and keep order; he did it in 1972, 1973 and 1974. He ran the drug side of the vice trade: selling, and letting people smoke on the spot; customers came from every class and place. Even the rats in the drug dens were addicted. The City was low-lying and flooded whenever it rained; the stalls should have moved up to the back lanes of Sa Po Road (沙埔道), but word could not spread fast enough, so they went on selling from a plastic tray floating on the water. He was later jailed for wounding someone and reformed through gospel drug rehabilitation. A 2023 Phoenix TV text says that he became addicted, then kept watch (巡場) at a drug stall in Sai Tau Tsuen (西頭村), south of the City.

people.name: Charles
people.story: Charles lived in the Walled City. Born in the City in 1959; his parents came from Hoiping (開平) after the Second World War and settled in the City. As a child he lived with his parents, grandmother and four siblings in a 400+ sq ft tin-roofed house, renting the second floor; the ceiling leaked every time it rained. His father worked in the bread trade, leaving early and coming back late, and alone supported a family of eight; his mother took casual work in the City. As children they watched adults throw dice in the City's big gambling dens (大檔) and peeped at strip shows from outside the cinema. He studied one year at Munsang College (民生書院), could not fit in, and left school. After leaving school at 12 he was an apprentice at a plumbing-and-electrical company; he soon quit to work with his father at a bakery on Nam Cheong Street, and later opened his own shop on Shanghai Street. After marriage he and his wife Maggie lived in a 5/F rear-block flat with no windows at all; his father bought a cheap second-hand flat in the City for the young couple. In 1985 the family had saved money and moved out before the clearance; he said the windowless, airless home made him determined to find a better place.

people.name: 莊澄
people.story: 莊澄 lived in the Walled City. He lived in the City as a small child, with his family. He lived there almost four years and left at age 7. Grown-ups stopped him from going to many places because of the vice dens, so the family went mostly to the main street and the stores (士多). His strongest memory is the building structure: a roof could suddenly appear in front of you. If you knew the way you could cross from roof to roof and be very hard to catch. He lived there with his family as a child and later advised the film's set builders.

people.name: 何生
people.story: 何生 lived in the Walled City. As a child he lived in Sai Tau Tsuen in the City, where tall buildings pressed tight against each other. In Sai Tau Tsuen you could still see the sky. Vice was far from him; the lanes crossed like a spider's web and you had to know the way. There was not enough water: residents sank their own wells ('scientific wells') and pumped groundwater. In the 1960s water rationing, everyone queued at the street tap in front of the village. In the evenings he and friends played badminton and football around today's Nga Tsin Long Road. He says firmly that the City was 'of course not a good place to live'. The first owner of 林記, 林生, was his elder sister's husband; the present owners call him 'uncle' (舅父). He started helping at 林記 in his teens: 'I am the first generation, I helped from start to end.' When 林記 was a street stall on Nga Tsin Long Road they slept on canvas cots by the goods for fear of heroin addicts stealing. In 1972 'the family' got public housing and moved to Mei Tung Estate. He was 75 in 2022 and still sat at the shop door greeting customers.

people.name: 林羅平's elder brother
people.story: 林羅平's elder brother worked in the Walled City. He had learned to make fishballs from age 9; when his younger brother 平哥 was in Primary 3, he and their mother rented a small ground-floor shop in the City and opened a fishball workshop, selling to markets and restaurants in other districts. There were no machines: they scraped the flesh off each fish by hand; 平哥 helped after school every day. Other fishball factories in the City waited for 平哥 and his brother to raise prices before raising their own. After the clearance he and 平哥 joined forces and moved to Fuk Lo Tsun Road (福佬村道).

people.name: 陳先生
people.story: 陳先生 lived in the Walled City. He and his parents lived in a high-rise on the outer edge of the City: more than ten storeys and no lift. Because there was no lift the rent was especially cheap, but water cost an extra HK$50 a month; the water meters in the City were said to be run by a private contractor. To save climbing the stairs, he phoned home before each trip back to ask what food or daily goods to buy.

details.text: He and his parents lived in a high-rise on the outer edge of the City: more than ten storeys and no lift.
Because there was no lift the rent was especially cheap, but water cost an extra HK$50 a month; the water meters in the City were said to be run by a private contractor.
To save climbing the stairs, he phoned home before each trip back to ask what food or daily goods to buy.

people.name: Johnnie To Kei-fung
people.story: Johnnie To Kei-fung (杜琪峯) lived in the Walled City. Born in a stairwell (樓梯底) on Tung Chau Street (通州街) and grew up from childhood in the City; left school in Form 3 at 17 and went to TVB as an odd-job boy. In the City he saw poverty, gangs and all kinds of people at first hand. Many of his neighbours in the City were gang members; he recalled that if the police were after you, you ran into the City and were safe. Born 22 April 1955.

details.text: The journalist gave him the name Cheng; it is not his real name.
He was about 40.
He was a former Nationalist policeman. He came to Hong Kong 14 years before 1963.
He built his 6-by-7-foot house from discarded lumber for his family of five. His wife and two small sons appear in the article.
He was the lookout of a small opium den in the City. The job paid 80 cents a day.
The den was open around the clock and served 200 customers a day from five pipes.

people.name: Lai
people.story: Lai was a friend of Cheng, the lookout of an opium den in the Walled City, in 1963. He was a former fruit peddler and had smoked opium for 15 years. He stopped once, but a stomach ailment made him start again. 'When I smoke,' he said, 'I feel no more pain and I can smile again.' He had no job: he tended the pipes of richer smokers and smoked their leftovers.

people.name: Chang Kat Kong
people.story: Chang Kat Kong was a Chiu Chow landlord and an air-conditioner repairer. He persuaded his Chiu Chow friends to pool their money and built his first 12-storey block of flats in the City. At the clearance he was paid HK$34.6 million for about 100 flats; he said that his own share was only HK$5 million. In 1993 he told the South China Morning Post: 'I'd rather still be running my air-conditioner-repair business at my Walled City shop and leading a happy and stable life.'

people.name: Mok Chung Yuk
people.story: Mok Chung Yuk worked for China Light and Power (中華電力) from the mid-1960s. In the late 1970s and early 1980s he was one of its engineers for the regulated supply of electricity in the Walled City. He did some of the very first surveys. At first the team dressed down, so that it did not look like an official team. The company brought its cable in from the outside, inch by inch. It rented about 250 square feet from the church in the City for a transformer, and in return it renovated the church's school. Permission for more substations came in 1984, and the work took three years. He declined to be photographed.

people.name: 袁家倫
people.story: 袁家倫 was a painter who came to Hong Kong from the mainland in the 1970s. In the Walled City, 袁家倫 rented a flat on the 13th floor, the top floor, and shared it with a colleague, Mr Li. The flat had a hall, three rooms, a toilet and a kitchen. The building had no lift and no telephone. Water came only from 3 pm each day, but a small bucket could take water from the tank on the roof. The flat shared one toilet, and often people queued for it. It also shared one kitchen, with one kerosene stove for each family. The roof was a place for exercise. The source does not give the years in the City. 袁家倫 left Hong Kong in 1992 and wrote the memoir 《火鳳凰》 (2020).

details.text: The flat was on the 13th floor, the top floor: a hall, three rooms, a toilet and a kitchen.
Water came only from 3 pm each day.
A small bucket could take water from the roof tank at any hour.
Each family had one kerosene stove in the shared kitchen; the rice cookers stood in the rooms.

people.name: Tam Sau-kuen
people.story: Tam Sau-kuen (譚秀娟) was a housewife in the Walled City. The Wall Street Journal (2014) quotes her about water. The City had no water supply for 24 hours a day. At any hour, even in the night, the sound of dripping water woke her. Then at once she did the housework, such as the laundry and the dishes. As a child she knew the area on Tai Chang Street (大井街) where the sex workers stayed. She said that it was dark 24 hours a day. The source does not give her years in the City or her address.
